issues.legal_issue: A statutory requirement to obtain executive consent before suing a ruler of a former state is constitutionally valid.
material_facts: The petitioner sought to challenge the validity of the requirement that he obtain government consent before filing a suit against a ruler of a former state.
The Court had recently upheld the validity of the requirement after considering its historical and legislative background.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge fails; the consent requirement is valid.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied its decisions in Narottam Kishore Deb Verma v. Union of India and Mohan Lal Jain v. Shri Sawai Man Singhji, which upheld the validity of Sections 86 and 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure in light of their historical and legislative background. It also noted that the requirement was out of tune with equality before law under Article 14 and might affect rights under Article 19(1)(f) and (g), making careful judicial scrutiny of consent orders necessary.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenges_pre_suit_: A person brings a constitutional writ challenging a requirement to obtain consent before bringing a suit.
predicates.suit_targets_former_ruler: The proposed suit is against a person who is a ruler of a former state.
predicates.consent_requirement_has_historical_legis: The consent requirement is part of a legal framework with a historical and legislative basis considered by the court.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges pre-suit consent for suing a former ruler and the requirement has the stated historical and legislative basis, the requirement remains constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: A person officially recognized as the successor of a ruler can qualify as a ruler for the purpose of the pre-suit consent requirement.
material_facts: The proposed defendant was the minor son and successor of a deceased ruler.
The President had recognized the proposed defendant as the successor of his father.
The proposed defendant had not signed the merger agreement himself.
issues.conclusion: The recognized successor qualifies as a ruler for the purpose of the consent requirement, notwithstanding that he did not sign the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Article 366(22) defines a ruler to include a person recognized by the President as the successor of a ruler who meets the definition's first part. The Court applied this inclusive definition in conjunction with Section 87B(2)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.consent_requirement_dispute_concerns_for: A dispute about applying a pre-suit consent requirement turns on whether the proposed defendant is a ruler of a former state.
predicates.person_is_presidentially_recognized_succ: The proposed defendant is officially recognized as the successor of a ruler.

issues.definition: When the dispute concerns former-ruler status and the proposed defendant is officially recognized as a ruler's successor, that person qualifies as a former ruler for the consent requirement.

issues.legal_issue: The executive authority deciding whether to consent to a suit against a ruler of a former state must not adjudicate the merits and should normally consent where the proposed claim raises justiciable and triable issues.
material_facts: The petitioner sought consent to bring a partition suit against a ruler of a former state.
The government refused consent for some properties on the ground that they belonged to the ruler and were not partible.
The government also rejected the petitioner's interpretation of a communication concerning the rights of third parties, thereby deciding disputed questions relevant to the proposed suit.
issues.conclusion: The government impermissibly adjudicated the merits; the consent authority should normally allow a suit raising justiciable and triable issues and should refuse consent only where the claim appears prima facie frivolous.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure, the consent power is intended substantially to protect former rulers from frivolous suits, not to transfer the civil court's function of deciding the merits to the executive. The Court relied on its guidance in Narottam Kishore Deb Verma v. Union of India that consent should not be refused casually and may legitimately be refused where the proposed claim appears prima facie frivolous. It also compared the possible dispute-avoidance function of Section 87B with the notice procedure under Section 80.

predicates.consent_application_for_suit_against_for: A litigant asks the executive for consent to sue a ruler of a former state.
predicates.proposed_claim_raises_triable_issues: The proposed claim presents justiciable issues that can be tried by a competent civil court.
predicates.executive_decides_disputed_merits: The executive resolves disputed questions about the merits of the proposed claim when deciding whether to consent.

issues.definition: If a consent application concerns a proposed suit against a former ruler, the claim raises triable issues, and the executive decides those disputed merits, the executive's merits determination is improper and consent should normally be granted.

issues.legal_issue: The executive authority cannot grant consent to a suit against a ruler of a former state only in part or subject to conditions, and a partial refusal based on adjudicating the merits cannot restrict consent to the suit.
material_facts: The petitioner sought consent to file one partition suit concerning properties listed in several schedules.
The government granted consent for some properties but refused it for others, relying on its view that the disputed properties were the ruler's non-partible private properties.
The government's affidavit showed that it would have consented to the whole suit but for its decision on the merits of the claims concerning the excluded properties.
issues.conclusion: The partial refusal was invalid; the order is to be treated as granting consent to the entire proposed suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 87B authorizes the government either to grant consent or to refuse it; it does not authorize conditional or partial consent, particularly where reliefs are claimed on one cause of action. Allowing conditions or partial consent would effectively confer on the executive authority to adjudicate the dispute, which is not the section's object. The Court also required meticulous scrutiny of refusals in light of the concerns about equality before law under Article 14 and possible effects on rights under Article 19(1)(f) and (g).

predicates.suit_against_former_ruler_seeks_relief_o: A proposed suit against a ruler of a former state seeks reliefs arising from one cause of action.
predicates.executive_grants_only_partial_consent: The executive grants consent for only part of the proposed suit and refuses it for the rest.
predicates.partial_refusal_rests_on_merits_adjudica: The executive's refusal for part of the suit rests on its decision about the merits of the claim.

issues.definition: When a proposed suit against a former ruler seeks relief on one cause, the executive gives only partial consent, and the partial refusal rests on a merits decision, the refusal is invalid and consent covers the entire suit.
